title: Mesoporous carbon from biomass walnut shell waste for energy storage applications: a green approach for waste to supercapacitor
abstract: Abstract The rising need for sustainable energy storage solutions has driven the investigation of carbon materials derived from biomass as environmentally friendly alternatives to traditional electrodes. Hence, we introduce an eco-friendly synthesis method to produce mesoporous activated carbon (WSAC) from walnut shell waste (WS) using a chemical-free hydrothermal process, addressing both waste utilization and renewable energy storage requirements. The WS precursor underwent cleaning, drying, and charring at 200 °C, followed by a hydrothermal treatment at 200 °C for 3 h to produce WSAC for supercapacitor applications. The WSAC exhibits a mesoporous structure, high active sites with improved electrochemical properties. Raman spectra analysis confirmed that WASC is composed of sp 3 hybridised graphite band (G band) and a high order of defective sites (D band) in the structure (I D /I G = 1.24). The WSAC exhibits a multilayer structure stacker together with a moderate specific surface area (138.32 m 2 g −1 ; BJH surface area is 25.589 m 2 g −1 ) and possess mesoporous nature (pore size is ∼2.34 nm). Additionally, TGA confirms thermal stability up to 500 °C, highlighting the material’s durability for practical applications. The WSAC shows the combination of pseudo-capacitance and electrical double-layer capacitance (EDLC) in three different electrolytes, including acidic (H 2 SO 4 , HNO 3 ), neutral (Na 2 SO 4 , KCI), and alkaline (NaOH, KOH) electrolytes. Interestingly, the WSAC electrode in alkaline electrolyte (0.5 M NaOH) at 1.4 V shows high areal specific capacitances of 4.17 F g −1 and high capacitance retention (63% for 3000 cycles), exhibiting superior performance than acidic and neutral electrolyte, related to a combined effect of EDLC and pseudo-capacitance mechanism This study demonstrates a cost-effective and environmentally friendly synthesis route to convert biomass waste into scalable, high performance electrodes for supercapacitor applications. It also contributes to the advancement of biomass-derived carbon materials for energy storage, aligning with global sustainability goals.
